questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I mainly looked at two things when choosing where to study abroad. First, I wanted to go to an English-speaking country and study at a university that was experienced in hosting exchange students. I thought this would make the administrative side of the exchange much easier, as there are many administrative steps to complete before even arriving, and it would also make it easier to follow the coursework. Second, I considered the location, weather, and culture. I wanted to live in a city with a good climate and experience a new culture, both through the university and in everyday life outside of it.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There was a welcome meeting in the first week of arriving, where your USYD study abroad advisor welcomes you and gives you a run down on supermarkets, banks, travel cards, apps that are good to have for finding your way around campus and getting deals on campus food. The following week there was a "welcome festival" with large events, free merchandise and stands with all clubs at the university.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
Quite difficult. Sydney housing is very expensive, and they are very late to post about housing opportunities. In general room/apartment listings are posted with less than a month to the move-in date. The contracts are normally for a year or sometimes 6 months if you're lucky. If you break the contract you have to pay a penalty, where the size of the penalty depends on how much time there is left of the contract. In my opinion the penalty was pretty steep. To avoid the penalty you can find someone to transfer the lease to, however, I never ended up going this route so I don't know much about it.  
I stayed at an airbnb the first couple of weeks of my exchange expecting to find housing in this time, however, I found it to be very stressful to have to find housing within such a short time frame. It does, however, allow you to see the areas which you are considering rather than just evaluating based on Google Maps which is nice. 
To find housing I recommend joining the Facebook groups 'Danskere i Australien - Danes in Australia', 'Danes in Sydney', 'Dansk i Australien', 'Young Danes in Sydney', 'Sydney - Houseshare / Flatshare / Room for Rent' etc.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
In general living near a metro station, train station or light rail station is ideal for getting around the city quickly and getting to and from campus with ease. In my opinion the buses are unreliable especially in rush hour as they fill up and stop taking in new passengers, meaning you have to wait for the next bus and hope that this one isn't full. They also stop very often making them quite a slow mode of transport. So using it for everyday transportation is a bit inconvenient. 
However, even if you end up living in an area which is a bit poorly connected you can get a Lime bike subscription pretty cheap, which makes biking around the city very accessible. Just know that you need to bike on the road along side cars for the most part, and that you have to wear a helmet by law. 
Personally, I lived near Waterloo metro station and found this very useful. The metro is also very new so it is very clean and has a large capacity for passengers. If you get a Concession Opal Card it also becomes very affordable to travel using public transport (you need an Australian address and it takes about two weeks to arrive though).

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: As I did not end up staying on campus, I can't say much on how it would be to live there. However, to get university housing it is a first-come first-served system which is sent out by email, but they sent the sign-up email out at midnight, which meant the university housing options were gone by the following morning.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Very easy, you can even change subjects in the first week of university (as long as you still get "merit" from KU).

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You sign up through a University of Sydney portal called 'Sydney Student Portal', where you can see which subjects have been approved, pending approval or declined approval.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Your University of Sydney study abroad advisor can also help you, however, they are normally pretty busy as they have a lot of students which they manage.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got most of the courses I wanted, however, the course "EDUH4052: Learning in Outdoor Education", which I really wanted was sadly cancelled for semester 1.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Read the course descriptions thoroughly, especially the 'assessment' section as it is pretty accurate at describing the workload expected of you throughout the course.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level was a bit easier than back home, however, assessments throughout the semester count towards your final grade, meaning you have to put in even effort throughout the semester to get a good grade. On the upside, this means if you do well on assessments during the semester you can make it impossible or nearly impossible to fail the final exam.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: There is not a lot of reading involved, at least in the courses I took. The material you need to know is presented in the lectures. Lectures are recorded and posted on Canvas on the same day, meaning you do not need to attend lectures physically. However, I still recommend keeping up with lectures as most courses have quizzes throughout the semester testing you on the course material thus far.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
HPSC1000: Bioethics - Very straightforward course, with 3x 1 hour lectures and 1x 1 hour tutorial a week (attendance is only necessary at the tutorial). The tutorial consisted of group discussions.
PCOL3012: Drug Design and Development - Recaps a lot of the material that we have touched on throughout the pharmacy bachelor, but also gives new perspectives on drug development. It is a good course to refresh your memory on organic chemistry. There are quite a few assessments throughout the course, which mostly are completed in groups (that are randomly made by course administrators). 
PHAR4815: Research Methods - Pharmacy students are put on this course to be able to transfer credits. We did not attend any lectures or tutorials for this course. The only two assessments were the final oral presentation in front of the cohort and the written assignment, which was handed in on canvas.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: HPSC1000: Bioethics was a very interesting course with a very manageable workload - would definitely recommend it to anyone studying science at KU.

questions.answer: My computer broke in the first week of university. There can be really heavy rainfall in Sydney, and this ended up getting through my bag and frying my computer. A raincoat/umbrella is definitely a good idea to have.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Housing is very expensive, but grocery shopping is less expensive.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Tennis, running, pickleball, paddle, surfing, swimming, bowing etc. There are endless sports and outdoor activities to try/join in Sydney.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Try a new sport either through the university clubs or just in the city.
Go to trivia nights at the bars! And a good way to hang out with new friends.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Manly the ferry ride over gives a great view of the opera house (see if you can spot 'Benny the seal' who hangs out on the back steps). The Spit to Manly walk is very nice or if you like snorkeling the Cabbage Tree Bay is a pretty cool spot. 

The Blue mountains either a day-trip or do a night or two. 

Do a walk out by Watson Bay, there are very nice views of the city from there. 

In the summer time WestPac openair is a pretty cool experience. 

Go to Glebe on a Saturday for the Glebe markets and go for lunch at the new Sydney Fish Market. 

Go on a surf camp (there are some advertised at university).

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Quite easy, Australians are very laid back :)

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I met locals through my courses. I would suggest picking third year or above courses as you are most likely to meet similarly aged students in these courses. Moreover, I would suggest not necessarily picking courses based on other exchange students, as this forces you to put yourself out there and talk to someone new!

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: How early the shops/cafes open and close. It is definitely a good city to live in if you are a morning person who likes to stay active.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Australians are very open, talkative and social people.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Try to stay on top of course work throughout the week, so that you have weekends free. Start writing your bachelors project early and try keeping a detailed journal of what you do in lab. 
2. If an opportunity presents itself to meet some new people - take it!
3. Take lots of photos!! Especially of the mundane things. Take pictures of the lecture halls, of the laboratory, of the new friends you make etc. When you get home it is so nice to have photos of the everyday things that were your 'normal' for half a year.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: To save some money get a Concession Opal Card early and get Revolut for easy money exchange.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Getting Australian friends!

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Finding housing.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Try Lee's dumpling in the CBD - very yummy xiaolongbao.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
